answer.rationale: The binding constraint is the 14-day expiry with no auto-renew while the line runs at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. That kills the two options the memory set makes most attractive on cost. memory_c2 (switch to the low-cost vendor) is the strongest cost lever on paper, but it is dated ('last year'), silent on volume and on whether onboarding was fast because there was slack; executing a primary-supply migration into a zero-buffer line in 14 days converts a cost win into a delivery-risk bet, which the primary objective forbids. memory_c3 (second source) is genuinely valuable but does not answer the expiry — dual-sourcing presumes a live primary contract, and here the primary lapses. memory_c5's defer precedent is explicitly scoped to a non-critical, month-to-month service; this contract is critical and has no continuation term, so that precedent does not transfer. That leaves the incumbent path, and memory_c1 supports it on stability but delivers nothing against the 18% mandate on its own. The distinction I am acting on: the incumbent refused to reopen price *this cycle*, which is not the same axis as memory_c6's multi-year volume commitment — term length is an unrefused lever, and memory_c4 says benchmarking has previously moved them on payment terms as well as price. So I intend a negotiated renewal, but sized as a guarded test rather than a full multi-year lock: secure continuity of supply plus a term-and-terms structure that books part of the 18%, while explicitly preserving the option to qualify the low-cost vendor next cycle. Two things I am not resolving and will not paper over: (1) I do not know whether the 18% target is reachable through term and payment terms alone — it may not be, and if verification shows memory_c6's volume pricing came from a different category or a much larger commitment than we can make, the honest read is that no single decision this cycle hits 18% without taking delivery risk; (2) the inherited memory set is visibly skewed toward incumbent-friendly outcomes with no recorded failures, which is a survivorship signal, not evidence that incumbent paths always work. The downstream risk I am flagging is lock-in: a long multi-year commitment bought for near-term margin entrenches single-vendor dependence and forecloses the memory_c2 and memory_c3 paths in later cycles, which is why I am capping commitment length rather than maximizing the discount. I am verifying memory_c6 and memory_c4 because they are the two records my chosen action actually rests on; if either turns out to be scoped to a different vendor or category, my action should change rather than proceed on inherited summary language.
